opening.headline: When you need to later prove who did what, you understand which records are made where and what they contain.
body: When a security or audit team asks, “Who uploaded files on this workspace last month?” memory or verbal explanations are not enough to answer the question. Proof is only established when there are records that can be retrieved after the fact.

In this class, we'll take a look at what columns Claude Enterprise's audit log consists of, how to export logs and how they differ from the Compliance API, and what the logs don't record. At the end, we will use the example of an audit request asking about activities from 8 months ago.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain what audit logs and compliance API are and how they are different
You can distinguish between what the log records and what it does not record.

screens.title: The moment you need to prove who did what
screens.lead: First, read three requests that really happen often in your organization. It's a good idea to read it and think about whether you can answer each request right away.

visual.alt: A scene where three question cards are arranged vertically and the phrase ‘records that can be retrieved after death’ is placed at the bottom.
labels: Who opened projects and uploaded files in this workspace last month?
When and who changed SSO settings?
Are there any records to prove the activity after the fact?
Proof = a record that can be retrieved after the fact

paragraphs: the security officer asks. “Can you show me who opened and uploaded files to projects in this workspace last month?” At the same time, the internal audit team requests the date the SSO settings were changed and who changed them.

Answering these questions by saying “I remember the conversation went well” does not provide evidence. This is because memories and verbal descriptions cannot be retrieved and checked. Proof is only established when there are records that can be retrieved after the fact.
This class covers where the records are made, what they contain, and what they don't contain. Know in advance what the records don't cover so you don't get embarrassed once the audit begins.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: There is a difference between having a record and being able to answer questions. By the end of the lesson, you will be able to explain this difference yourself.

screens.outro: First, let's think about your organization's experience.

screens.title: When was the last time you opened the audit log?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: When was the last time you opened the audit log?
items.answer: In many organizations, audit logs are first opened only after a problem occurs. If you have never opened it before, you will start without knowing what kind of heat it will produce at the moment you need it and for how long.

items.prompt: Whose actions were you looking for at that time?
items.answer: See if what you're looking for is organized into people (who), actions (what), and objects (where). These three are the basic framework of an audit log. In the following screens, see how this skeleton corresponds to the actual column names.

items.prompt: Was the information you wanted in the log or not?
items.answer: If not, the log may have been turned off, the retention period may have expired, or the log may contain a type of information that it is not intended to contain. Since the solutions for the three cases are different, we will distinguish them one by one in this lesson.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's take a look at what a single line of logs looks like.

screens.title: Structure of the audit log: actors, events, targets
screens.lead: Below is an article explaining the column configuration of the audit log. When you select a highlighted passage, an explanation of what each column answers appears.

visual.alt: An illustration of one line of the audit log divided into five columns, with each column corresponding to who, when, what, and what.
labels: ip_address, device_id, user_agent, client_platform: recorded together when applicable

data.text: The audit log consists of the following columns: created_at, actor_info, event, event_info, entity_info. It is created_at is the time the log was recorded., and it is actor_info is information about the actor, and it is event is the type of event. It is entity_info is the entity affected by the event. In addition, The ip_address, device_id, user_agent, and client_platform columns are recorded together where applicable. occurs.

marks.span: created_at is the time the log was recorded.
marks.note: This is the column that serves as the basis for chronological reconstruction. Sort by this column to answer when it happened. Without vision, the sequence of events cannot be proven.

marks.span: actor_info is information about the actor
marks.note: This column answers who did it. Information that identifies the actor, such as an email address, is included. It is written that in system events where the actor is unknown, it may be empty, so documentation is provided only when possible.

marks.span: event is the type of event
marks.note: This is the column that answers what happened. Event names are logged, such as conversation creation (conversation_created), file upload (file_uploaded), and SSO connection activation (org_sso_connection_activated).

marks.span: entity_info is the entity affected by the event
marks.note: This is the column that answers what was affected. It contains types and unique identifiers (uuid) such as accounts, invitations, projects, conversations, files, and SSO connections. Names are recorded together only when possible.

marks.span: The ip_address, device_id, user_agent, and client_platform columns are recorded together where applicable.
marks.note: A secondary column that shows which network address, device, program, or mobile platform (iOS or Android) the action came from. This is used to check if the same person is connected from an unfamiliar device.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the structure of a single line of logs, let's compare the way to actually retrieve this log.

screens.title: How to get your logs out: Export and Compliance API
screens.lead: Select each tab to see the differences in who can use each log, how far back it goes, and what it contains.

tabs.label: Export Administrator
tabs.body: In Claude Enterprise, Owner and Primary Owner export audit logs using the "Export logs" button in the Data & Privacy menu of Organization Settings. Logs from the last 180 days are collected at the time of request. A download link will be emailed to the owner who requested the export, and the link is only valid for 24 hours. It may take time to collect logs, so your email may be delayed.

tabs.label: Customer Managed Key Organization
tabs.body: Organizations using customer-managed encryption keys on the Enterprise plan cannot export using the "Export logs" button. This organization receives audit log events into the Compliance API. Just because you don't see the export button or doesn't work doesn't mean there isn't a log. The path is just different.

tabs.label: Compliance API
tabs.body: The Compliance API brings an Activity Feed into your program. The activity feed queries `GET /v1/compliance/activities` and requires a key with the range `read:compliance_activities`. The response consists of `data`, `has_more`, `first_id`, and `last_id`, and each activity record contains information such as the actor's email and IP address. Claude Enterprise also supports viewing content such as chat, files, and projects.

tabs.label: OpenAI Compliance Platform
tabs.body: OpenAI's Compliance Platform can be used in ChatGPT Enterprise and Edu workspace and provides immutable, append-only log events. You can connect these logs to eDiscovery, DLP, and SIEM tools. To access, a workspace owner or administrator must create a workspace-scoped Admin key with the necessary permissions.

screens.outro: Now that we've established that different paths have different scopes and durations, let's apply them to our case.

screens.title: Case explanation: Why there is no proof even though there is a log
screens.lead: The instructor explains a case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Example: Audit request asking for a conversation from 8 months ago
steps.body: The audit team asked, “Show me who posted what files in a conversation from 8 months ago.” Your organization has an audit log and can also write administrator exports. Let's ask three questions to see if this request can be answered with logs alone:

steps.title: Step 1: Check the time period
steps.body: Administrator export only collects logs from the last 180 days at the time of request. Since 8 months ago is approximately 240 days ago, the records will not be available through this route. Checking the period is the first judgment.

steps.title: Step 2: Check what the log contains
steps.body: In the audit log, titles and contents of chats and projects cannot be exported; only unique identifiers are exported. So, even though logarithm can tell “who created what conversation,” it cannot answer “what was said in that conversation.”

steps.title: Step 3: Find a separate route to obtain content
steps.body: The input and output of the chat can be received by the Primary Owner through data export. Organizations using the Compliance API can retrieve chat and file contents through content inquiry. In other words, the log gives clues and other paths prove the content.

steps.title: Step 4: Consider the retention period and storage entity
steps.body: OpenAI's Compliance Logs Platform retains data for 30 days and advises users that if they wish to keep it longer, they must continue to download and retain it according to their own policies. If you only rely on the provider's retention period, old records will disappear.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: The mere existence of a log is not proof. Three things must fit the question: period, scope, and storage entity. This case is a question that is over 180 days old and requires content, so it cannot be answered with just one log.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the limitations through examples, let us move on to the process of preparing evidence in advance.

screens.title: Explanation of the Collection Process: Evidence Begins with Settings
screens.lead: As you select each step, the instructor explains your role and the consequences of missing that step. Notice that proof starts with setup.

items.prompt: Step 1: Turn on the Compliance API
items.answer: In Claude Enterprise, the Compliance API can only be turned on or off by the Primary Owner in the API menu in Organization Settings. Owners can see this page, but cannot see the activation toggle, and Admins cannot see the page itself. If you miss this step, no one will be able to use your API.

items.prompt: Step 2: Determine the range and create a key
items.answer: In the key creation page on the same page, the Primary Owner can create a key that includes all connected organizations, and the Owner can create a key that is scoped to his or her organization. If you only need an activity feed, a key with the range `read:compliance_activities` will suffice. Giving only as many permissions as needed will reduce the damage if your keys are leaked.

items.prompt: Step 3: Connect to your security tool
items.answer: When you connect your keys to a security tool like a SIEM, Claude activity comes into your dashboards and workflows like any other application. Because security teams see events in the tools they already use, audit requests don't require any manual work.

Records cannot be restored after the provider's retention period. Before you start collecting, you need to decide how long, where and who will keep it. Without this policy, old records will be empty even after connecting to the tool.

items.prompt: Step 5: Accept that there is no history before turning it on
items.answer: Logs are records that are accumulated when turned on. If you turn on the setting after an audit request has been made, only the activity after that will remain. So having your proof ready means getting it set up and stored before the request comes.

screens.outro: Let me conclude with the conclusion that a gap in procedures is a gap in evidence.

screens.title: Proof begins with setup
screens.lead: Let’s group together what we’ve seen so far into one standard. Read the paragraph below and move on to the final summary.

paragraphs: Audit logs leave information about who (actor), what (event), and what (entity) was done along with time. The NIST glossary describes an audit trail as a record that allows activities to be reconstructed chronologically. These three elements and perspectives must be in place to reconstruct an event.

However, the log does not contain the content of the conversation itself, but only identifiers. If content is needed, a separate path must be used, such as data export or content inquiry in the Compliance API. Distinguishing between what the log records and what it does not record is the key to this lesson.

The scope of evidence is determined by the export period (180 days for Claude), the provider's retention period (30 days for OpenAI), and when the organization initiates its own archiving. All three of these come from settings and procedures. So proof begins the moment you turn on the log and decide to archive it, not after the incident has occurred.

For example, if the request asks about the last month's activities, just exporting it is sufficient, but if the request asks about activities or conversations from a year ago, the answer depends on whether or not you have self-saved it in advance. Remember that the required path will vary depending on the timing and type of request.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: There are three questions to ask when you are asked to audit: What period is it, does the log contain its contents, and who keeps it?

checks.intro: Check out the log structure you just saw. Just match each column with the question it answers. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match the columns in your audit log with the questions they answer.
right: What is affected: Types and UUIDs of projects, files, SSO connections, etc.
Who did it: Information like email, IP address, and device ID
A column that uses when it happened as the basis for chronological reconstruction
What Happened: Event Types Like Login, SSO Login
checks.correctFeedback: The roles of the four columns are clearly defined.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some of the connections between columns and questions were misaligned. Break it down again into who, when, what, and to what.
checks.explain: An audit trail is a record that links actors, events, and objects chronologically, allowing activity to be reconstructed. Perspective becomes the standard of order, and actors, events, and objects answer who, what, and what, respectively.

checks.intro: Apply the judgment process from the case study again. All you have to do is read the situation and choose the most accurate decision.
checks.q: The audit team asks, ‘Who uploaded what files in the conversation 8 months ago?’ What is the most accurate decision when trying to answer only Claude Enterprise's log export?
options: Since the log contains the title and content of the conversation, you can fully respond by exporting it.
Since the export only contains the most recent 180 days, records from 8 months ago will not be exported through this route.
If you export with Admin privileges, all past records will be displayed without retention period restrictions.
If you open the export link within 24 hours, the entire record will open regardless of the time period.
checks.correctFeedback: It is correct to consider the period limit first.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This choice incorrectly assumes the duration or scope of the export.
checks.explain: The export only contains the last 180 days. Additionally, since logs contain unique identifiers rather than conversation content, the contents must be secured through separate data export or Compliance API content inquiry.

wrong.0: The log only contains identifiers, not the conversation title and content.
wrong.2: Export is requested by the Owner and is not subject to any time restrictions.
wrong.3: 24 hours is only the validity time of the download link and has nothing to do with the recording range.

glossary.def: It is a record of who (actor), what (event), and what (entity) was done along with the time. It serves as a basis for reconstructing activities after the fact.
An API for administrators to import content such as activity feeds, chats, and files into the program. It is used by security, legal, and compliance teams for auditing and sub-tool integration.
This is the period during which logs can be viewed or exported. Claude's admin export is 180 days, OpenAI Compliance Logs Platform is 30 days.
This is a record that can be taken out to prove an action after the fact. Even if there is a record, the period and scope must match the question to be evidence.
It is a security tool that collects logs from multiple systems, analyzes them in real time, and finds threats. Compliance API data can be connected and used.

misconceptions.myth: If there is a log, all conversations will be proven.
misconceptions.fact: In the audit log, titles and contents of chats and projects cannot be exported; only unique identifiers are included. The content must be obtained through a separate path, such as data export or content inquiry from the Compliance API.

misconceptions.myth: If you turn it on when you need it, past records will also appear.
misconceptions.fact: Logs accumulate as long as they are turned on, and cannot be restored after the provider's retention period. You need to decide in advance how long you need proof and start setting up and storing it.

misconceptions.myth: Any administrator can turn on the Compliance API.
misconceptions.fact: Only the Primary Owner can turn the Compliance API on and off in Claude Enterprise. Owners can create keys but cannot see the toggles, and Admins cannot see the page.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Proof begins with the settings, where you turn on logs and decide on their retention.
Audit logs capture the visuals of actors, events, and objects, but do not contain the content of their conversations.
The export period and the provider's retention period determine the scope of evidence available.
Compliance API and self-archive are a means of bridging the limitations of timescale and scope.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What questions can't be answered right now from my organization's logs? Try to determine which of the following is lacking: period, content, or storage entity.
